Point 3 of the algorithmic review recorded on roll-lqjj.14 remains present on main cdf311f1af0c6066bd6bef32f9540d034312f45d, checked against fetched origin/main on 2026-10-15. No existing implementation task covers it.

Evidence: crates/beadroll-core/src/replay/apply/create.rs:48 retains every uid in State::awaiting on every create and calls materialise_dangling for each waiting issue. materialise_dangling (:166) scans all of that issue's remaining unresolved dependencies. State::awaiting is still a Vec<EventId> (state.rs:108). Skipping issues with no unresolved dependencies helps the ordinary case but leaves quadratic work when every create adds another issue with a missing target, even when no awaited key arrives.

The original release probes on roll-lqjj.14 measured 8,000/16,000 creates with one unresolved dependency each at 3.02/12.36 seconds, versus 10/23 milliseconds without unresolved dependencies. These are historical measurements from 2026-10-13, not measurements rerun during this investigation.

Index waiting dependencies by their target key so a create visits only the matching work. Consider edge-level indexing or an equivalent arrangement so one issue awaiting many different keys does not have all its remaining dependencies scanned for every arriving key. Preserve the existing binding semantics: actual assigned keys after collision renaming, self references left unresolved, normalized dependency types, imported metadata, import-create tags, and removals by key/type or target uid with their causal rules. Hash iteration must not affect observable order.

The index must remain correct through full replay, projection extension, and projection encode/decode. Relevant seams include replay/apply.rs:240 (dep_remove) and projection/state_codec.rs:72,111 (awaiting persistence). Follow the crate's projection encoding rules if stored representation changes; format 1 and replay outcomes stay unchanged. Existing coverage includes hardening::v4_dangling_replay_determinism, hardening::g14_key_retraction_lost_to_concurrent_target, and projection::tests::finished.

This is separate from the completed import-planning lookup optimization roll-lqjj.15 and projection finishing optimization roll-lqjj.17.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- Unrelated creates do not scan all waiting issues or unresolved edges; resolving many different keys on one issue does not repeatedly scan its entire unresolved list.
- Differential coverage preserves edges, dangling entries, metadata and output order for forward targets, duplicate/multi-type references, self references, key collisions and both forms of retraction, including concurrent target creation. Full replay, extended projections and decoded projections agree.
- Record reproducible release-mode before/after measurements at 8,000 and 16,000 issues for never-arriving targets, targets arriving later, and a single issue awaiting many keys; include the no-unresolved-dependency control. Demonstrate removal of the quadratic scan without wall-clock test gates.
- Update the review decision and findings ledger, plus user-facing guarantees if affected; the fast baseline is green and the change is on main.
fields.title: Index unresolved imported dependencies by the key they await

fields.description:
Point 4 of the algorithmic review recorded on roll-lqjj.14 remains present on main cdf311f1af0c6066bd6bef32f9540d034312f45d, checked against fetched origin/main on 2026-10-15. No existing implementation task covers it.

Evidence: crates/beadroll-core/src/query.rs:202 open_blockers allocates and sorts a complete blocker list and walks ancestors for each issue. is_blocked (:235) calls it just to test emptiness, and State::ready (:242) repeats that for every candidate. The CLI has its own ready path in crates/beadroll/src/commands/list.rs:90-113, so optimizing State::ready alone would leave the command unchanged. commands/queries.rs:14-33 filters blocked issues through is_blocked and then constructs the blocker lists again; view.rs:131 also asks for the boolean in every detail.

The original release probes on roll-lqjj.14 measured a 2,000/4,000-issue parent chain at 407/1,678 milliseconds. These are historical measurements from 2026-10-13, not measurements rerun during this investigation.

Compute and reuse a cycle-aware boolean analysis for one immutable State/query batch, with work approaching O(N+D) before result sorting. Keep full blocker enumeration for callers that display the actual blockers; its output size can itself be large. Wire both public-core and CLI bulk callers through the shared analysis without changing readiness rules or making a single-issue query unnecessarily costly.

Semantic constraints from open_blockers: direct blocks targets count only when not done; disputed closed/tombstone statuses are not done; only an epic waits for its own unfinished direct children. Ancestor inheritance carries prerequisites, not an ancestor's epic-child waiting rule or merely its status. Traversal stops at done ancestors, follows every parent link, excludes revisiting the queried issue, and terminates on merged cycles without recursion overflow. Scope restricts membership only: an outside prerequisite or second parent still blocks an inside issue. Preserve claim/status filtering, result order and CLI limits.

Existing tests in commands/ready_subtree.rs, commands/deep_tree_review4.rs, and core replay/readiness coverage provide compatibility anchors. Keep the reverse-dependency rendering optimization in point 5 independently actionable.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- State::ready and the CLI ready path share analysis across candidates; bulk boolean consumers reuse it where applicable. Boolean checks do not build complete blocker lists per issue.
- Differential tests against the existing blocker semantics cover deep chains, shared/multiple parents, merged parent cycles, done and disputed ancestors/targets, epic versus non-epic children, inherited prerequisites, claims and blockers outside a scoped subtree. Blocker-list contents/order and ready output/filter/limit behavior stay unchanged.
- Record reproducible release-mode before/after measurements on 2,000/4,000 and larger parent chains plus a shared-ancestor graph, excluding fixture setup. Show graph analysis no longer grows quadratically; distinguish analysis from result sorting and required blocker-list output. Timing is evidence, not a test gate.
- Update the review decision and findings ledger, plus user-facing guarantees if affected; the fast baseline is green and the change is on main.
fields.title: Share cycle-aware readiness analysis across issues

fields.description:
Point 5 of the algorithmic review recorded on roll-lqjj.14 remains present on main cdf311f1af0c6066bd6bef32f9540d034312f45d, checked against fetched origin/main on 2026-10-15. No existing implementation task covers it.

Evidence: crates/beadroll-core/src/view.rs:201 dependents iterates every issue, collects and sorts its dependency keys, then filters for the requested issue uid. detail (:97) invokes this for every issue. Multi-issue callers still repeat detail: commands/show.rs:18-20, commands/update.rs:106-110, and commands/ownership.rs:151-155 (claim/takeover results). The child index only handles parent-child relationships and does not replace this all-types reverse lookup.

The original release probes on roll-lqjj.14 measured all details on a sparse graph of 4,000/8,000 issues at 540/2,328 milliseconds. These are historical measurements from 2026-10-13, not measurements rerun during this investigation.

Build a reverse-dependency index once per state snapshot or detail batch and reuse it for requested issues. Preserve dependents in source-issue replay order, with each source's matching edges in sorted-edge order. Retain one output per distinct (target uid, dependency type), all dependency types and statuses, the existing treatment of empty/removed tags and unresolved targets, and the current field/JSON ordering. Index by stable uid so key collisions/renames cannot misdirect edges. Output remains in the caller's requested issue order, including duplicate requests and existing error behavior.

Choose an ephemeral batch view or maintained derived index based on measured cost; no public event-format or ownership-protocol change is needed. Avoid making single-detail calls cost more than their existing one pass, and retain the core detail API's established behavior for consumers. If an index is persisted, follow projection encoding and rebuild rules. Point 4's readiness analysis is a separate bottleneck within detail and must not be conflated with the reverse-dependency measurement.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- Multi-issue show, update and claim/takeover result construction build/reuse the reverse index once per state snapshot, rather than scanning and sorting all issues' dependency edges for every requested detail.
- Equality tests preserve detail objects and their ordering for replay order differing from uid/key order, multiple types between the same pair, duplicate tags, removed edges, dangling dependencies, closed/deleted sources, renamed keys, duplicate requested ids and relevant CLI errors. Existing public single-detail behavior remains compatible.
- Record reproducible release-mode before/after sparse-graph measurements at 4,000 and 8,000 issues for all details, with fixture setup excluded and a single-detail control. Use a graph without ancestor walks to isolate reverse lookup; demonstrate one graph pass plus matching-edge/output work rather than one pass per detail. Timing is evidence, not a test gate.
- Update the review decision and findings ledger, plus user-facing guarantees if affected; the fast baseline is green and the change is on main.
fields.title: Reuse a reverse-dependency index when rendering multiple issue details

data.text:
Reinvestigated all five candidates on 2026-10-15 against clean main cdf311f1af0c6066bd6bef32f9540d034312f45d, which matches fetched origin/main.

1. Addressed by closed roll-lqjj.15: import.rs builds created_keys and resolves dependencies through hash lookups; planning and dry-run validation share resolves. Ledger Z01 and import compatibility tests document the change.
2. Addressed by closed roll-lqjj.17: transition still requests state between closes, but Projection::extend calls finish_some, which skips labels and child-index rebuilding for closes, and advance inserts new ids into a BTreeSet without sorting the full history. Ledger Z02/V01/V02, projection::tests::finished and timing --extend cover this. The documented whole child-index rebuild for a create or dependency change remains an accepted separate limit.
3. Still present: every create scans State::awaiting and every waiting issue's dangling dependencies. Filed roll-lqjj.18.
4. Still present: is_blocked builds open_blockers and repeats ancestor walks across candidates, including the separate CLI ready path. Filed roll-lqjj.19.
5. Still present: detail calls dependents, which scans/sorts dependency edges across every issue, once per requested detail. Multi-show, update and ownership output repeat it. Filed roll-lqjj.20.

All three follow-ups are open P2 tasks under roll-lqjj, with current code references, preserved semantics, behavioral and release-probe acceptance criteria. The performance numbers in their descriptions are explicitly attributed to this original 2026-10-13 review; they were not rerun during this investigation. No repository files changed.

Baseline ./check.sh on the unmodified checkout: 862 tests run, 860 passed, 2 failed, 3 skipped; doctests passed (0 cases), all 14 infra tests passed. Both failures reproduce in a targeted rerun: commands::review6::git_helper::f15_timeout_reaps_the_git_helper (commands/review6/git_helper.rs:65) and hardening::v1_run_git_timeout_hygiene::timeouts_leak_nothing_and_reap_as_documented (beadroll-git/tests/git/hardening/v1_run_git_timeout_hygiene.rs:99). Both assertions concern helper processes remaining after timeout. Log: target/check/tests.log. This investigation did not modify or diagnose the timeout implementation.

Implemented on local main (not pushed) in e364de1, 1439239, 68b93e0 and be67b21, reviewed by Codex over cdf311f..be67b21. State::awaiting (state/awaiting.rs) lists every waiting imported dependency by the key it names, its issue and a number fixed when its list began to wait: a create takes the entries its key settles and visits nothing else, a removal by key finds an issue's entries the same way, an entry taken out holds its place as null until the finishing pass (finish / finish_some) makes the list whole, and survivors are never listed again. The index is derived (projection::ENCODING 4; a state read back numbers each list afresh). Replay outcomes are unchanged: projection::tests::awaiting has scenarios for forward targets, duplicate and multi-type references, self references, a rename beside a removal in the same batch, removals by key and by target, and concurrent target creation, each through replay, extension one record at a time with and without read-back, and one batch, plus a digest of 30 seeded histories pinned from cdf311f's replay; all of them also pass on cdf311f. cargo xtask timing --dangling N, back to back at 8,000 / 16,000: never-arriving 4.50 / 30.28 s -> 0.044 / 0.093 s; arriving later 2.02 / 7.94 s -> 0.038 / 0.084 s; one issue awaiting all 1.57 / 9.05 s -> 0.24 / 0.78 s; control 0.021 / 0.045 s -> 0.019 / 0.046 s; the same issue's keys taken one create a batch by a projection 1.26 / 5.08 s -> 0.38 / 1.52 s. Review round 1 found F1 (ledger W01): entries listed by place were re-listed on every batch (10.13 / 50.68 s on that last shape); fixed in be67b21. Round 2: no findings. ./check.sh green (878 passed, 3 skipped), fmt and clippy clean. The one-issue shapes still grow as N squared because an issue's edges are a VecMap searched in order (roll-dih8.11), filed as a follow-up.

fields.description: Found while closing roll-lqjj.18, measured on main at be67b21 (local) on 2026-10-15. Issue::dep_tags is a VecMap (crates/beadroll-core/src/state/small.rs, roll-dih8.11) searched in order, so each new edge (replay::apply::create::bind for an import, at its create or as a waited-for key arrives, and dep_add) scans the issue's edges, and replay::finish_some's parent-child index rebuild walks them again each batch. cargo xtask timing --dangling N measures it: one issue given every other's key at once (one_has_many) took 0.141 s at 8,000 and 0.498 s at 16,000, the same before and after roll-lqjj.18; one issue waiting for every other's key took 0.24 s and 0.78 s after it; an experiment that left the edge insertion out brought the latter to 0.034 s and 0.066 s. The representation was chosen because an issue mostly has a few edges (roll-dih8.11, heap budget), so a fix must keep the small case's memory: for example a VecMap that builds a lookup once it grows past a threshold, for dep_tags or for every VecMap.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- Adding the N-th edge to one issue costs less than a scan of its edges once an issue has many, for bind and dep_add alike; edges keep their order and metadata, and replay, extended and decoded projections agree.
- cargo xtask timing --dangling N shows one_has_many and one_awaits_many growing about linearly from 8,000 to 16,000, before and after recorded; the replay heap budget at 200,000 events (timing --replay) still holds.
- docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 and docs/FINDINGS.md updated; the fast baseline is green.
fields.title: One issue given N dependency edges costs N squared: its edges are a vector searched in order

data.reason: A create now visits only the imported dependencies waiting for its own key, and a removal by key only an issue's entries for that key: State::awaiting lists each waiting entry by key, issue and a number it keeps, and a list made whole after a batch lists nothing again (Z03; review finding W01 fixed). Replay outcomes are unchanged, as the scenario tests and a 30-history digest that also pass on cdf311f show; extended and decoded projections agree with replay. Projection ENCODING is 4. Back to back at 16,000: never-arriving keys 30.28 s -> 0.093 s, arriving later 7.94 s -> 0.084 s, one issue awaiting all 9.05 s -> 0.78 s, control 0.045 s -> 0.046 s. The remaining N-squared growth of one issue's N edges is its VecMap (follow-up roll-lqjj.21). Commits e364de1..be67b21 on local main, not pushed; ./check.sh green; Codex review converged in round 2.

data.text: Implemented on main as three commits, be67b21..6abf4ea: ad3efe8 (State::readiness judges every issue at once; State::ready, the CLI's ready, blocked and prime ask it once; State::is_blocked stops at the first thing found; open_blockers unchanged; differential tests replay::readiness and commands::shared_readiness), a47eab4 (cargo xtask timing --ready N), 6abf4ea (REVIEWING §2 decision, FINDINGS Z04, GUARANTEES known limit, CHANGELOG). Verification on this checkout, Rust 1.99.0: cargo fmt --check and clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings clean; ./check.sh green (892 tests passed, 3 skipped, doctests and 14 infra tests passed). Release probe (fastest of 3, 64 cores): held chain analysis 0.9/1.8/4.3/11.2 ms at 2k/4k/8k/16k issues vs complete lists per issue 0.43/1.74/7.12/33.3 s; free chain ready (with sort) 0.4/0.8/2.3/10.4 ms vs analysis 0.2/0.5/0.9/4.6 ms; lattice analysis 1.0/2.0/5.9/13.7 ms vs lists 0.63/2.62/12.6/90.2 s. End to end on a scratch store against the base's bead (best of 5; 3 at 16k): chain-4000 ready 2.05 -> 0.037 s, blocked 4.05 -> 2.14 s (the lists it prints), prime 2.04 -> 0.035 s; lattice-4000 ready 3.59 -> 0.046 s; chain-16000 ready 37.0 -> 0.149 s, blocked 76.5 -> 35.4 s; show and list unchanged. Codex review (gpt-6-astra, xhigh, read-only) of the pinned range reported no actionable defects. Not pushed: the commits are on local main only.

fields.notes: Discovered from roll-lqjj.19 while adding timing --ready N. The USAGE text in xtask/src/main.rs lists every timing mode (--replay, --sync, --read, --merge, --contend, --import, --plan, --extend, --ready, --load) but not --dangling N, which roll-lqjj.18 added to timing.rs, the module doc and xtask/AGENTS.md without a usage line or a description sentence. Acceptance: USAGE gains a 'timing --dangling N [--label NAME] [--out FILE]' line and a sentence saying what it measures, matching the module doc of xtask/src/timing/dangling.rs; cargo xtask help shows it. Low severity, documentation only.

data.reason: Readiness is judged once for every issue: State::readiness (crates/beadroll-core/src/query/readiness.rs) finds the issues that are not done and have a prerequisite of their own, then everything not done that reaches one through parents that are not done, by one walk down the parent-child index; State::ready and the CLI's ready, blocked and prime ask it once a command, State::is_blocked stops at the first thing found, and open_blockers still lists the blockers for bead blocked. Rule, lists, order and limits unchanged, kept by replay::readiness (chains, shared parents, cycles, done and disputed statuses, epics, claims, scopes, 80 random graphs) and commands::shared_readiness. A chain of 4,000 issues is judged in 1.8 ms where the lists took 1.74 s; bead ready there 2.05 -> 0.037 s, at 16,000 37.0 -> 0.149 s (cargo xtask timing --ready N; REVIEWING §2, FINDINGS Z04, GUARANTEES, CHANGELOG). ./check.sh green (892 passed, 3 skipped); Codex review of be67b21..6abf4ea found no defects. On local main at 6abf4ea, not pushed. Follow-up roll-lqjj.22 filed for the usage text omission noticed on the way.

Every shown issue's dependents are found at once: State::dependents_of (crates/beadroll-core/src/view/dependents.rs) reads every issue's edges once for all the issues a command names, keeping and sorting only the edges naming one of them by uid text, and State::detail_with lists each one's; bead show, update, claim and takeover make it once a command. State::detail of one issue is still one pass, comparing targets with its uid instead of hashing (half the old lookup's time), and a lookup from another state is never used. Dependents, their order, detail order, duplicate ids and ISSUE_NOT_FOUND where it stands are unchanged, kept by replay::dependents (60 random graphs among the cases, against detail alone and the old reading, member for member) and commands::shared_dependents (also green against the base binary). timing --details N: all details 20/49/95 ms at 4k/8k/16k vs 0.49/1.92/8.87 s each alone; lookup 3.0/8.1/17.0 ms vs 0.67/3.42/18.4 s; bead show of all 4,000 0.85 -> 0.13 s, 8,000 3.26 -> 0.28 s, same bytes (REVIEWING §2, FINDINGS Z05, GUARANTEES, CHANGELOG). ./check.sh green (905 passed, 3 skipped); Codex review of 6abf4ea..8683332 found no defects. On local main at 8683332, not pushed.

fields.description: Review 16 is a performance follow-up review of 4d7e03e..8683332 (roll-lqjj.15 to roll-lqjj.20). It found no correctness bug in that range and seventeen findings, ids X01 to X17: quadratic work left one step away from what the range fixed (bead blocked's lists, the blocked flag of several details, renamed copies), and where a command's time now goes (a projection switched off for good by one integrity entry, cache files fsynced, repeated projection decodes in online writes, per-attempt-file passes, journal-loading commands, show's git processes per closed issue, teardown, discovery's gits), plus guards and two design questions. This issue records the report under docs/reviews/ and a Review 16 section in docs/FINDINGS.md with every X row open; each fix lands under its own child issue and pull request, which sets its rows.
fields.acceptance_criteria: docs/reviews/2026-10-15-16-claude-performance-follow-up.md holds the report: what was checked and how, each finding with its evidence and measurement, ranked; docs/FINDINGS.md has a Review 16 section (ids X) with X01-X17 as open rows; the fix issues and their pull requests are named; docs only, the baseline's hygiene tests pass.

fields.description: X01: bead blocked builds each held issue's list with State::open_blockers (crates/beadroll/src/commands/queries.rs:28), each walking the issue's ancestry, so a deep hierarchy costs issues x depth: a held chain of 16,000 takes 43.2 s and of 4,000 2.05 s. X02: show, update, claim and takeover of several issues judge each detail's blocked with State::is_blocked (crates/beadroll-core/src/view.rs:146): show of every issue of that chain takes 28.7 s. Z04 left the lists where they are printed and Z05's probe had no parents, so neither saw this. X12: sort_for_listing allocates a String per comparison (4.3 ms against 3.1 ms for 20,000 issues). A prototype (blocked-lists.patch: Tarjan over the not-done parent graph, inherited sets shared; one Readiness for several details) makes the chain's blocked 0.26 s and show 0.62 s with byte-identical output. Evidence and measurements: /home/aa/.cache/beadroll-review16/ (review-notes.md, sweep-notes.md), the review 16 report once roll-lqjj.23 lands.
fields.acceptance_criteria: bead blocked lists every held issue's blockers in one pass over issues and edges plus the size of what it lists, equal for every issue to open_blockers (keys in key order), on deep chains, lattices, merged parent cycles, done and disputed ancestors and targets, epics, scopes and random graphs; several details share one readiness judgement and State::detail of one issue is unchanged; listing sorts without allocating; outputs byte-identical; xtask timing --ready measures the lists both ways; docs and ledger rows X01, X02, X12.
fields.title: List every held issue's blockers at once, and judge readiness once for several details

fields.description: X03: replay renames a copy whose key another machine minted too by State::free_key, which builds claimed_keys(), a set of every issue's key and every key an import waits for, once per copy (crates/beadroll-core/src/state.rs:275): two machines importing the same 8,000-record export offline, then syncing, rename 8,000 copies, and the second machine's sync takes 6.6 s and a cold replay 4.7 s, against 1.15 s for the same creates with nothing renamed. The awaiting index of roll-lqjj.18 already lists every awaited key: with by_key and that index asked per candidate (free-key.patch), 2.7 s and 1.1 s. Evidence and measurements: /home/aa/.cache/beadroll-review16/ (review-notes.md, sweep-notes.md), the review 16 report once roll-lqjj.23 lands.
fields.acceptance_criteria: free_key asks of each candidate whether an issue has it or an import waits for it, without collecting every key; the keys chosen are unchanged, which tests show against claimed_keys on replayed states and histories with renames and waiting imports; a probe measures a replay renaming N copies against its control; docs and ledger row X03.
fields.title: Find a renamed copy's key by lookups rather than by collecting every key for each copy

fields.description: X08: bead show answers each closed issue's merged with merged_into_default (crates/beadroll-store/src/place.rs:43), about five gits per issue, the default branch resolved again each time: 100 closed issues take 4.1 s and 1,000 29.8 s; resolved once and asked together (merged-batch.patch), 80 ms and 131 ms, output byte-identical. X14: where.commit comes from any machine's event and reaches git unchecked: a NUL fails show of that issue with IO, a leading '-' is read as an option, revision expressions such as HEAD~1 or :/regex are evaluated. Evidence and measurements: /home/aa/.cache/beadroll-review16/ (review-notes.md, sweep-notes.md), the review 16 report once roll-lqjj.23 lands.
fields.acceptance_criteria: show resolves the default branch's refs once a command and asks each distinct commit once, in a fixed number of git processes for the hex commits bead records; merged is unchanged for merged, unmerged, missing and empty commits and issues named twice (a test of several closed issues passes before and after); a NUL or a leading '-' never reaches git as an argument and answers unknown; whether a commit that is not hex should answer unknown is decided and recorded in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2; docs and ledger rows X08, X14.
fields.title: Ask git whether closed issues are merged once a command, and keep journal text out of git's options

fields.description: X05: write_atomic always fsyncs (crates/beadroll-store/src/fs.rs:91), so the command after every write flushes the projection and appends to its text file with an fsync, as the journal is. Both are caches bead rebuilds whenever they are missing, cut or damaged, and every part is read against its sum. Unflushed (floor.patch), the read after a write takes 9.5 ms instead of 39.1 ms on 300 issues and 42 ms instead of 74 ms on 5,000 (medians, interleaved); a write cycle about halves on Linux. data.reason: Discovery starts the committed .beadroll.json's git cat-file --batch together with git config (origin's URLs) and the combined git rev-parse, instead of after both had answered: Git::run_alongside (crates/beadroll-git/src/alongside.rs) runs any number of gits with the one it waits for, Checkout::origin_urls takes the caller's extra git, and discover.rs's may_read_committed guesses from the start directory upwards whether the cat-file may be needed (the nearest .git has no .beadroll.json beside it, a repository itself, none found, GIT_DIR or GIT_WORK_TREE set). Its answer is used only where git's own top has no .beadroll.json, so every answer, warning and error is unchanged, including the early-error paths (a dangling link or a file that is not JSON is refused first and starts no cat-file); a wrong guess costs an unused git or a cat-file started after the others as before. The same gits run (3 for a read, 2 with a file in the tree, 4 for a local write by strace -f -e trace=execve), only their order changed; capture_where's rev-parse HEAD --abbrev-ref HEAD stays under the store lock, where the branch an event records is read. Release builds, one issue, 30 interleaved runs in six sets on a shared machine at load ~11 (absolute figures inflated: list took ~21 ms against the review's 6.2): the fastest was 0.7 to 2.2 ms lower after in 17 of 18 sets of list, show and a local comment (list 21.9 -> 20.5 ms, show 22.4 -> 20.8, write 31.8 -> 30.1 in the first set), the medians within the noise. Tests: children::discovery_reads_the_committed_configuration_only_where_the_tree_has_none (passes against the base binary up to its GIT_DIR case, which only the new code satisfies), beadroll-git's alongside and checkout unit tests; ./check.sh green (906 passed, 3 skipped), fmt and clippy clean (REVIEWING §2, FINDINGS X11, crates/beadroll-git/AGENTS.md, CHANGELOG). The projection and its text file, checksummed caches bead makes again from the journal, are no longer fsynced: fs::write_cache_parts (crates/beadroll-store/src/fs.rs) writes them whole and renames them into place, with the atomic-write and atomic-written failpoints firing as before, and projection save() and the text file's start() and append() use it; journal segments, attempts, pending files, receipts, meta.json, replica.json and the journal memo stay fsynced, and answers, both files' bytes and format 1 are unchanged. Why a crash can only cost a replay is written in REVIEWING §2's durability bullet: the projection's lengths and three sums, the text file's header against the generation the projection names, and each text's bytes against the place and sum the projection kept mean a lost, cut, zeroed, stale or out-of-step file is never read as current (FINDINGS X05, GUARANTEES, CHANGELOG, store AGENTS.md). A renamed copy's key is found by lookups: State::free_key asks State::claims_key of each candidate (crates/beadroll-core/src/state.rs), which is by_key holding it or the awaiting index naming it (Awaiting::names, one range lookup in the set arrived and retract keep), instead of collecting claimed_keys() for each copy; claimed_keys stays public with its answer, mint_key still collects it once a command. Design summary (br-outline, early; full design with figures follows). Measured on ec773f9, release, in process, plain history at 200,000 events (19,939 issues, 88,152 named events): decode_state 97 ms, heap 73 MB; state part 14.0 MB, index 5.4 MB. By phase (TSC-timed, instrumented): issues ~73% (dep_tags 29 ms / 2.4 MB, registers 19.5 ms / 2.4 MB, ownership history 16 ms / 1.1 MB, fields 10 ms / 2.8 MB), the named events' records ~22% (causes 13 ms / 1.6 MB, machine+actor+table 12.5 ms), finishing (relabel) ~5%. A reader asks the event table only for who wrote the entries of a register with several entries (State::conflicts): 176 of 88,152 events here.
Steps, each a change of projection::ENCODING only, format 1 unchanged:
1 (my PR): the event records (causes, machine, actor) move from the state part to the index; the state part keeps chain breaks and the writers of the events behind registers with several entries. Reads: about -20% decode, -3.3 MB state bytes, -12.6 MB heap. Writes: the same work, from the index.
2: typed dependency edges: the target an issue id (16 bytes) or text, the kind interned, the metadata of each addition kept with the texts (only show/export print it).
3: ownership history (ended claims, lost claims, stale ends) kept with the texts, read in by show/export.
4: short fields shown from their registers, as long fields are (roll-lqjj.10), each value held once.
The outline part is what the state part becomes once 1-4 have moved out what list/ready/blocked/prime never read; no second state type.
Assumed of br-rewrite (X17): the projection stays parts (made, state, index, texts) with the state part read alone by reads; whatever you do to how much of the index a write rewrites, the event table can live in the index (or a part of its own beside it) and a reading decode never needs it. Step 1 does not depend on your layout; tell me if you plan to move the event table yourself.

Design summary, early (br-rewrite; full design with every measurement follows). Measured on main (ec773f9, release, shared machine) at 200,000 events, end to end: a write with nothing to extend 281 ms; the read after it 295 ms against 169 ms for a read with nothing to extend; a write after a write 387 ms. The 126 ms a write adds to the command after it is almost all the save: encode 94 ms, assembling and summing the 19 MB 10-19 ms, writing it 6-8 ms; decoding the index costs only 26 ms over the state's decode, and extending by a record 0.25 ms (12 us a record, about 50 ns a byte of tail, against about 6 ns a byte of projection for a save).
Step 1 (my PR, no change to the projection's bytes, so no ENCODING bump needed for it): a command that extends the projection in order to write (projection(ws): Tx::new, the merge, info, machines) no longer saves it until the records applied after the stored one hold more than a 64th of its bytes; a command that reads (state/outline) still saves whatever it extended, since a reader with a tail must decode the index (26 ms) every time. Writes after writes stop paying the 106 ms save; no read gets slower; the save happens less often, never differently, so crash and race behaviour is the one already argued (renamed whole, unflushed, read against sums).
Later steps (each its own issue): the write keeps its transaction until exit instead of freeing it (83 ms a write at 200k; X10's ground); encode skips recomputing named/kept knowledge (45 ms of the 94) and compacts only now and then; encode copies the stored bytes of issues and events it did not touch (needs per-issue self-contained bytes: joint with br-outline's layout); append-only parts so a save writes what changed.
What I assume of br-outline: Projection::decode/extend/encode keep their contracts; the stored file stays one file renamed whole with summed parts; a decode for extension still needs the index. My step 1 does not touch the layout, so it does not depend on yours.
Added the timed X03 growth guard (timing::growth); PR #18 updated.

Step 2 of roll-lqjj.35's design (X16, review 16): a reading command decodes the whole state whatever it prints; this step makes the dependency edges it decodes cost what readiness, blocked, list --parent and show read of them. Follows roll-lqjj.35's design (see its comments for the measurements and the order of steps); a change of projection::ENCODING only, format 1 unchanged.

What it does: each dependency edge's target is held typed, an issue's id (16 bytes, no allocation) or the text of a target that names no issue, and its kind interned (the projection's name table, an Arc<str> shared by every edge of that kind) instead of two Strings per edge; the metadata each addition carries ({created_at, created_by} and whatever an import brought), which only bead export prints, moves to the issue's texts (roll-lqjj.6), read in where export and a later event need it, as long fields are. Issue::deps and Issue::dep_tags give the same answers in the same order; readiness, blockers and dependents stop parsing every target as an id.

Measured on ec773f9 (release, plain history, 200,000 events, 19,939 issues, 17,975 edges): dep_tags are the largest phase of decode_state, about 26% of it (TSC-timed, instrumented), and 2.43 MB of the 14.0 MB state part. Expected: that phase to a third or less (about -15% of the decode, after roll-lqjj.35's step 1 about 7 ms of 44 ms in process), -1.3 to -1.6 MB of the state part, and readiness/ready (9 ms / 12 ms) a little cheaper. Risk: medium. Issue::deps' key type (String, String) is used across core and the CLI (dep, update, list --parent, export, views); the change touches replay's edge code and the texts codec, and goes with roll-lqjj.21 (edges a vector searched in order), which changes the same structure: do them together or this first. The differential tests (projection against replay, read back half the time), projection/tests/finished.rs (rewires) and the golden/commands tests keep it; extend read_back to compare each edge's metadata once texts are read in, and add a test that export and show print the same bytes with the metadata read from the texts.

Acceptance: decode_state of the 200,000-event plain history measurably faster (cargo xtask timing --decode 200000, before and after, back to back), every command's output byte for byte, docs/REVIEWING.md §2 and docs/FINDINGS.md X16 updated.

data.text: PR: https://github.com/bpcakes/beadroll/pull/19

Design (br-outline, X16): what a reading command decodes, measured, and the order of steps. Each step is a change of projection::ENCODING only; format 1 is unchanged by every one.

HOW MEASURED. ec773f9, release builds, Linux x86_64, 64 cores shared with three other agents (absolute figures inflated; only runs made together are compared). Plain history of `cargo xtask timing` (six machines). In process: `cargo xtask timing --decode N` (added by step 1's PR: decode_state, Projection::decode, the heap a decoded state holds, bytes of each part, fastest of 7) and a scratch probe (ported from the review's decode-probe.rs) that times each phase of decode_state with the TSC (the clocksource here is HPET: Instant::now costs about 1.4 us, so per-issue laps with it were meaningless) and counts the bytes written by each part. Phase times are TSC-timed with the instrumentation in (the sum is about 112 ms against 57 ms clean), so read them as shares. End to end: `cargo xtask timing --read N`, base and step 1 back to back.

DECODE BY PHASE, 200,000 events (19,939 issues, 17,975 edges, 88,152 named events), share of decode_state, and bytes of the state part (13.99 MB):
- issue dep_tags: 26% | 2.43 MB (targets as 36-byte uuid text, kind a String, each addition's metadata an object of two strings)
- issue registers: 17% | 2.41 MB (title, priority, assignee, and the status register's object of status/closed_at/close_reason: the values the fields hold again)
- issue ownership (claim, claim_history, provisional, lost, stale): 14.5% | 1.09 MB
- events' causes: 11% | 1.64 MB
- events' machine, actor and the table (an Arc and an IndexMap entry each): 11% | 0.26 MB; their ids 0.7% | 1.41 MB
- issue fields: 9% | 2.76 MB (16 slots of 32 bytes; title, status, type, assignee, dates as strings)
- relabel (labels derived from label_tags): 4%; label_tags 2.6% | 0.35 MB
- uid+key 1% | 0.51 MB; by_key 0.51 MB; texts' places 0.44 MB; origin/where 0.12 MB; the rest small. Awaiting index and children index 0.4 ms each.
Index 5.44 MB: ids 3.20 MB, ancestry 2.24 MB. Texts 2.0 MB.
Heap of a decoded state: 73.0 MB: issues 55.9 MB (an Issue is 976 bytes inline, 512 of them the fields array), events 12.6 MB, by_key 1.8 MB, derived (awaiting, labels, children) 2.7 MB. Freeing it 93 ms (no longer paid by a reading command since X10).
At 20,000 events (1,990 issues): decode_state 5.0 ms, state part 1.40 MB, index 0.50 MB, heap 7.4 MB; the same shares.
Ownership-heavy 200,000 (14,578 issues, 51,594 named events): decode_state 70 ms (instrumented probe), state 12.6 MB; text-heavy 200,000: 101 ms, state 14.9 MB, texts 54.6 MB. The shares are alike.

WHAT EACH COMMAND READS. list: key, title, status, priority, issue_type, assignee, labels, where.branch, the disputed fields (registers with several entries; who wrote them only in show), created_at, updated_at, and edges of kind parent-child for --parent; ready/blocked/prime: those plus every edge's target and kind, the children index, the claim; claims: the claims; show/update/claim/takeover: everything of the issues named, every issue's edges (dependents) and readiness; export/search/lint: everything. Only show-like commands and export read the ownership history, only export an edge's metadata, and only conflicts (show) ask who wrote an event: at 200,000 events 176 of the 88,152 named events sit behind a register with several entries (8 of 51,594 in the ownership-heavy history).

OPTIONS WEIGHED.
- An outline part as a second, smaller state type for list/ready/blocked/prime: rejected. Every query (readiness, blocker_lists, brief, sort_for_listing) is written against State and Issue; a second type means two implementations of readiness or a trait over both, and the differential tests would have to compare three things. The same effect comes from moving out of the state part what those commands never read, step by step, the way roll-lqjj.6 moved the texts: the state part becomes the outline.
- Lazy decode (each issue's bytes decoded on first access): rejected for now. It needs interior mutability in an Issue a State shares across threads (Send + Sync is a contract of the crate), and every reader of all issues (list, ready) still decodes all of them.
- Causes dropped from the projection altogether: the clocks already imply most of them (dropping them at read-back failed no existing test), but saw_at reads them first and they are the only answer for a cause that was never observed (quarantined ids); not worth a proof now: kept, in the index.
- The three steps of the issue, plus the events' records and the ownership history, which the review did not name and are 22% and 14.5% of the decode.

STEPS, IN ORDER (expected gains are against the decode of the moment, at 200,000 events in process).
1. Event records out of the state part (this PR). The state part keeps the writers (machine, actor) of the events behind registers with several entries, and chain breaks; the index holds every named event with its causes, machine and actor, and the machines. Measured: decode_state 56.6 -> 43.8 ms (-23%), heap 73.0 -> 60.4 MB, state part 13.99 -> 10.68 MB, index 5.44 -> 8.75 MB; Projection::decode 64 -> 63 ms (a write does the same work). End to end (timing --read, best of two rounds of five, back to back): 200,000: list 0.146 -> 0.121 s, show 0.150 -> 0.116 s, ready 0.201 -> 0.157 s; info, machines and a local write unchanged within noise (0.29 -> 0.28 s); 20,000: list 19.6 -> 16.4 ms, show 19.5 -> 16.4 ms, ready 22.3 -> 19.7 ms. Projection file 19,449,049 bytes where 19,445,469 (each part its own name table). Risk: low; no type changes, every answer from the same data; the differential tests' read_back now checks both parts (and fails when the index loses the causes, which nothing caught before).
2. roll-lqjj.39: dependency edges typed (target an issue id or text, kind interned) and each addition's metadata with the texts (only export prints it). Expected -15% of the decode, -1.3 to -1.6 MB. Risk: medium (Issue::deps' key type is used across core and the CLI; replay's edge code). Goes with roll-lqjj.21 (edges a vector searched in order), which changes the same structure: together, or this first.
3. roll-lqjj.40: ownership history (ended claims, lost claims, stale ends) with the texts, read in by show/update/claim/takeover/export and before applying records about the issue. Expected -12%, -1 MB. Risk: medium (every reader of the history must read texts in).
4. roll-lqjj.41: short fields shown from their registers, as long fields are (roll-lqjj.10); the issue keeps only what no register holds. Expected -12 to -15%, -2 MB, -10 MB heap. Risk: medium-high (replay's representation of every short field; the differential tests cannot see a semantic change, so a test of every field against today's copy-out comes first).
After all four, the estimate: decode_state about 20-25 ms at 200,000 events where it was 57, the state part about 6 MB where it was 14: a read costs what list/ready print, plus what parsing a status and a title costs.
Order: by gain over risk, and by independence: step 1 changes no type and only which part holds the event table, so it does not depend on X17's layout; 2 and 3 use the texts mechanism of roll-lqjj.6 and change what an issue's texts hold; 4 is last because it changes replay itself.

WHAT I ASSUME OF br-rewrite (X17, roll-lqjj.36).
- The projection stays in parts whose state part a reading command reads and sums alone: whatever you do to how a write saves the rest (an appended tail, parts saved when changed, ids out of the rewritten bytes), decode_state needs only that part. Step 1 makes the state part smaller and the index larger by the event table (3.3 MB at 200,000), so the event table is now index data: if you split the index into parts saved apart, the event table can be its own part (it changes with every write, as the ids do, but is kept compacted to the events the state names).
- Extension: a decode for extension must still read the full event table with causes, from the index (Projection::decode). I change nothing about when the extended projection is saved; if you extend from the journal's tail without saving, a reading command that extends must still produce a State whose knowledge has the writers its conflicts ask about: Projection::extend keeps every event in its knowledge, so it does.
- Your step 1 (reads that extend still save; writes save once the tail passes a 64th) fits: a read that extends decodes the index, which now holds the event table, and its State keeps every event, so its conflicts' writers are there.
- Your later "encode copies the stored bytes of issues it did not touch" needs per-issue self-contained bytes; today names and shared values (machines, actors, places) are written once per part and referred to after (codec::Writer::name/shared), so an issue's bytes are not self-contained. Nothing in my steps depends on that sharing: step 2 interns edge kinds, which can be per issue or a fixed table of known kinds plus text, whichever your layout needs; tell me before either of us lands the other.
- Steps 2 and 3 add to what an issue's texts hold, so they change the text file's contents but not when or how it is appended: they assume texts stay an append-only file read by place and sum.

fields.description: Follows roll-lqjj.36's design (X17), step 2. A write frees its transaction, which holds the whole projection with its index, once the store lock is let go (roll-lqjj.32, X10): still inside the process, 83 ms of every write at 200,000 events (strace of an offline comment: decode ~185 ms, append and fsync, then 83 ms freeing, 17 ms exit), about 6 ms at 20,000. Keep it until the process exits as a read keeps its state (Outcome::answered_from), freeing it first only when the command publishes, so that no command holds two. Expected gain: ~83 ms a write at 200,000 events; output, format 1 and the projection unchanged; no projection::ENCODING change. Risk: low (memory held until exit; run_with and libraries free as before).
fields.title: A write keeps its transaction until the process exits

fields.description: Follows roll-lqjj.36's design (X17), step 3. Every write-back runs named() over every issue and Knowledge::kept over every event (24 + 29 ms of the 94 ms encode at 200,000 events), though a projection read back and extended holds exactly the kept events plus the batch's. Record in the index how many events the knowledge held when it was last compacted, and compact again only once it holds an eighth more; between, a write-back writes the knowledge as it is. Expected gain: up to ~45 ms of every write-back at 200,000 events (the read after every write included), ~4 ms at 20,000. Risk: medium: the knowledge then holds events the state no longer names, which conflicts and who() must not read; extend the differential test to compare with it. projection::ENCODING bump.
fields.title: Compact the projection's knowledge now and then, not at every write-back

fields.description: Follows roll-lqjj.36's design (X17), step 4; joint with roll-lqjj.35 (X16), which owns which part holds what, after its layout steps. encode re-encodes every issue and every event record whatever the batch changed (49 + 21 ms at 200,000 events, 0.25 ms to apply the record). Make each issue's and each event record's bytes self-contained in their part (the name and shared-value tables a part of their own, appended to), keep an offset table, have extend mark the issues and events it changed, and have encode copy the rest from the stored bytes. Expected gain: most of the remaining 50-70 ms of encode at 200,000 events (the copy ~3 ms). Risk: medium-high. projection::ENCODING bump.
fields.title: Write back a projection by copying the bytes of what the write did not touch

fields.description: Follows roll-lqjj.36's design (X17), step 5; joint with roll-lqjj.35 (X16). A write-back writes the whole 19 MB file and sums it (8 ms of sums, 6-8 ms of writing, 10 ms assembling at 200,000 events), the 3.2 MB of event ids among it. Keep the issues, event records and ids in an append-only file like the text file (roll-lqjj.6), placed and summed by a small root that alone is renamed whole: a write-back appends what changed and rewrites the root (~1 MB at 200,000 events); the ids are appended, never rewritten (the issue's 'keep the event ids out of what is rewritten', ~7 ms alone, not worth a step of its own). Expected gain: ~15-20 ms of every write-back at 200,000 events, and its bytes from 19 MB to about 1 MB. Risk: high: a second cache file the durability argument (REVIEWING §2, roll-lqjj.27) must cover, compacted like the text file. projection::ENCODING bump.
fields.title: Append-only projection parts, so that a write-back writes what changed

data.text:
Design (br-rewrite, roll-lqjj.36, X17): when the projection is written and how much of it each write rewrites.

HOW IT WAS MEASURED. Release builds of main (ec773f9) on a machine shared with three other agents, so absolute figures are inflated and only runs made back to back are compared. In process: the review's decode-probe.rs ported to ec773f9 (scratch, not committed) on the plain history, best of 5, with an instrumented copy of Projection::decode/encode for the sub-phases. End to end: the store `cargo xtask timing --read N` builds, kept (scratch patch), and a script after writebench.py that times on it a write after a read (nothing to extend), the read after it, a read again, and a write after a write; strace -tt for where each command's time goes.

THE CYCLE BY PHASE, main, in process:
| phase | 20,000 events | 200,000 events |
| bytes (state / index / texts) | 1.40 / 0.50 / 0.20 MB | 13.99 / 5.44 / 2.00 MB |
| decode_state (a read) | 8.6 ms | 92-118 ms |
| Projection::decode (state + index: a write, or a read with records to apply) | 9.4 ms | 144 ms |
|   of which the knowledge index / ids read / ids into the set | 0.6 / 0.1 / 0.3 ms | 23.4 / 0.8 / 2.2 ms |
| extend by 1 record | 0.06 ms | 0.25 ms |
| extend by 10 / 100 / 1,000 / 4,000 records (parse + apply) | 0.2 / 1.2 / 12.3 / 50 ms | 0.3 / 1.4 / 12.2 / 52 ms |
| encode | 8.6 ms | 94 ms |
|   of which named / kept (knowledge compaction) / issues / event records / index / ids | | 24 / 29 / 49 / 21 / 2.7 / 1.2 ms (of a fresh projection; less on a decoded one) |
| assemble + sum the 3 parts, write + rename (not fsynced since X05) | 1.9 ms | 8 ms + 6-8 ms |
| free the projection | 6.4 ms | 104 ms |
So extending costs about 50 ns a byte of tail (12 us a record), and writing a projection back about 6 ns a byte of projection.

End to end, main, at 200,000 events (best of 5 / median): a write after a read 281 / 303 ms; the read (show) after it 295 / 315 ms; a read again 169 / 174 ms; a write after a write 387 / 415 ms. At 20,000: 39.3 / 40.1, 34.0 / 34.5, 21.5 / 22.1, 49.2 / 51.1 ms. strace of the write at 200k: ~185 ms reading and decoding the projection with its index, 20 ms `git rev-parse`, the segment append and its fsync, then 83 ms freeing the transaction after the lock (X10 put it there), 17 ms process exit. Of the read after it: 32 ms reading and summing the file, 153 ms decode with index + extend, 85 ms encode, 19 ms appending texts, assembling and summing, 6 ms writing 19 MB, 12 ms freeing what it wrote; the rest (meta.json and the memo for the unpublished count, ~75 ms here, outside X17) as in any read. So what a write adds to the command after it, 126 ms at 200k and 12.5 ms at 20k, is almost all the write-back; the index decode is 26 ms of it.

THE OPTIONS, WEIGHED.
- Extend from the journal's tail without saving until the tail is long. For a command that writes, a longer tail costs 50 ns a byte, against a write-back of 6 ns a byte of projection: deferring is nearly free. For a command that reads, a tail costs the index decode (26 ms at 200k, about a fifth of a write-back) on every read until someone writes it back: a ski-rental where reads after a write would lose after about five reads, and a reader cannot count reads without writing something. So: readers keep writing back what they extended; writers defer, until the tail holds more than a 64th of the projection's bytes (then the last write before a write-back spends about an eighth of a write-back on the tail, a run of writes about a sixteenth a write on average). No change to the bytes: no ENCODING bump needed. Crash and race: the projection is written less often, never differently; a deferred tail is exactly what a killed or failed write-back leaves today, already handled by the grown/appended rules and Y01 (the stored file only gets older, so its identities only get more settled). Concurrency: fewer writes of a shared cache; a writer that defers takes no text-file lock. THIS IS STEP 1.
- The write saves its own projection (under the lock): moves the encode from the read to the write, saves only the reader's index decode (26 ms), and lengthens the lock. Rejected.
- Save only the parts that changed. Needs encode to stop re-encoding untouched issues and events (issues 49 ms + events 21 ms of encode at 200k) and the compaction pass (named + kept, ~45 ms) to stop running every time; then the bytes written to follow. Steps 3-5.
- Keep the event ids out of what is rewritten: 3.2 MB of 19 MB, but only ~1 ms to encode, 3 ms to decode, 1.6 ms to free, ~1.5 ms of sums and writes at 200k (about 7 ms of the 126). Not worth a step alone; folded into step 5.
- Better found: the 83 ms free of the write's transaction (X10 moved it outside the lock but kept it) is the largest single phase a write pays after its decode. Step 2.

THE STEPS, in order (each a change of projection::ENCODING at most, format 1 unchanged):
1. (this PR) A command that extends the stored projection to write (projection(ws): Tx::new, a merge, info, machines) writes it back only once the records it applied hold more than a 64th of its bytes; a command that reads (state, outline) writes back whatever it extended. Bytes unchanged, no ENCODING bump. Gain: a write after a write at 200k stops paying the write-back (~106 ms of 387 ms); nothing else moves. Risk: low; the write-back happens less often, never otherwise.
2. (roll-lqjj.42) A write keeps its transaction until the process exits, as a read keeps its state (Outcome::answered_from), freeing it first only when it publishes. Gain: ~83 ms a write at 200k, ~6 ms at 20k. Risk: low (memory held to exit; no command holds two). No ENCODING change.
3. (roll-lqjj.43) Knowledge compacted now and then: a write-back of a decoded projection does not rerun named + kept over every event; the index records how many events the knowledge held when it was last compacted, and a write-back compacts again once it holds an eighth more. Gain: up to ~45 ms of the 94 ms encode at 200k, on every write-back (reads after writes included). Risk: medium (knowledge holding events the state no longer names; the differential test must compare against replay with that knowledge, and conflicts/`who` must not read them). ENCODING bump.
4. (roll-lqjj.44) Encode copies the bytes of what extension did not touch: each issue and each event record self-contained in its part (the name and shared-value tables as a part of their own, append-only), an offset table, and extension marking the issues and events it changed; encode copies the rest from the stored bytes. Gain: most of the remaining ~50-70 ms of encode at 200k (the copy ~3 ms). Risk: medium-high. Joint with br-outline (X16 owns which part holds what): after br-outline's steps 1-4 settle the layout. ENCODING bump.
5. (roll-lqjj.45) Append-only parts: the issues, event records and ids in an append-only file like the text file, placed and summed by a small root that is the only file renamed whole; a write-back appends what changed and rewrites the root. Gain: write-back bytes from 19 MB to the root (~1 MB at 200k) plus what changed, and the sums with them (~15 ms at 200k); the ids are then appended, never rewritten. Risk: high (a second file the X05 argument must cover, compaction of that file like the text file's). Joint with br-outline. ENCODING bump.
After 1-5 at 200k the read after a write would cost about what a read with nothing to extend costs plus the index decode and the tail (~175-200 ms against 295 ms today), and a write about 190 ms (281 today) before br-outline's decode work.

ASSUMED OF BR-OUTLINE (roll-lqjj.35): Projection::decode/extend/encode keep their contracts (a decode for extension still reads state and index; extend applies a batch as replay would after every event held); the stored projection stays one file renamed whole with summed parts (step 5 is where that changes, jointly); your step 1 (event records moved from the state part to the index) is compatible with every step here and steps 3-4 take it as given. Step 1 here does not touch the layout or the decode, so it does not depend on yours and you do not depend on it. I do not plan to move the event table myself.

MEASURED GAIN OF STEP 1 (release, main ec773f9 and the branch back to back, best of five; the machine shared, so compare only pairs): `timing --read 200000`: write after write 0.375 -> 0.259 s; write after read 0.258 -> 0.262 s and read after write 0.273 -> 0.281 s (noise: the same work); list/show unchanged. `timing --read 20000`: write after write 0.048 -> 0.036 s, others unchanged. `timing --sync 200000`: sync after a local write 0.506 -> 0.339 s, write published at once 0.803 -> 0.643 s (the merge no longer writes the write's record back); at 20,000 0.133 -> 0.117 s and 0.169 -> 0.167 s. Interleaved cycle (7 runs, min/median): 200k write after write 395/405 -> 279/298 ms; 20k 50/55 -> 40/42 ms; reads unchanged. writebench.py (write then show, 20 interleaved, medians): 300 issues 25.1/8.4 -> 24.4/8.6 ms, 5,000 issues 47.6/41.5 -> 47.0/40.5 ms: unchanged, as expected (each write there follows a read). Differential: a second track extends the projection last written back by every batch since at once (store order): 1,053 such extensions of 2-19 batches in the 40 clean seeds, 378 in the flawed ones, and 10,000 flawed histories (many_seeds, release) all equal to replay.

key::free_key (crates/beadroll-core/src/key.rs:29-39) counts a numbered key (stem.N) upward from N, asking State::claims_key of each candidate until one is free. Found by the independent review of PR #18 (guard for X03, roll-lqjj.38); predates it. X03 (roll-lqjj.25) made each ask a lookup, so a copy of a plain key asks a bounded number of keys, but a copy of a numbered key asks about every number already taken above it.

Scenario: two machines that each mint the children ex-1.1 to ex-1.N of one parent before they sync. Replay renames the second machine's N copies; the keys asked of (counted as Work::Key, work::tally) are 1,640 at N=40, 6,480 at 80, 25,760 at 160 and 102,720 at 320: 62.6x for 8x the copies, so quadratic. In a debug build the test-only check that every ask agrees with the keys collected makes it cubic: 2,000 such copies hit nextest's 300 s timeout. Not guarded: work/tests/renamed.rs uses plain keys (ex-N) and docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 lists the case among the exceptions by design until this is fixed.

Direction: for a copy of a numbered key, start from where the last numbered rename of that stem stopped (a per-stem next number held by the state, or found by a range lookup over by_key for the stem), keeping the keys chosen byte for byte as free_key chooses them now (the lowest free number above the key's own), so replay of a journal renames to the same keys; format 1 is frozen. Then add the numbered shape to work/tests/renamed.rs and to the nightly growth guard.
fields.acceptance_criteria: Replay of two machines' N copies of ex-1.1..ex-1.N asks a number of keys growing linearly in N (work::tests::renamed guards it at 250 and 2,000 copies), chooses the same keys as before, and REVIEWING section 2 no longer lists it as an exception.
